walkthrough:
**Write what decomposition means**

Think simply. Heating splits the hydrogen halide into its elements. It is the $\text{H-X}$ bond in the compound that has to be broken.

$$2\text{HX(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \text{X}_2\text{(g)}$$

**Decide which bond controls stability**

Stability depends on how hard it is to break the bond that is present in the starting compound. That is $\text{H-Cl}$ in $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{H-I}$ in $\text{HI}$, not the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ or $\text{I-I}$ bonds which are only formed in the products.

**Compare H-Cl with H-I strength**

Chlorine is smaller than iodine, so the $\text{H-Cl}$ bond is shorter with better orbital overlap. Bond strength decreases down Group 17, so $\text{H-Cl}$ is stronger and has a higher bond energy than $\text{H-I}$.

**Pick the more stable compound**

A stronger bond needs more thermal energy to break, so $\text{HCl}$ resists decomposition much better than $\text{HI}$. That is why $\text{HI}$ decomposes on gentle heating while $\text{HCl}$ is stable to high temperatures.

options.A: The identity is right, hydrogen chloride is more stable, but the explanation is wrong. The $\text{Cl-Cl}$ and $\text{I-I}$ bonds are in the products, not in the compound being broken, so they do not determine how easily $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{HI}$ decomposes.
options.B: Correct on both parts. Hydrogen chloride is more thermally stable because the $\text{H-Cl}$ bond is stronger than the $\text{H-I}$ bond due to smaller size, shorter bond length and better overlap, so more heat is needed to break it.
options.C: Both parts are wrong. Hydrogen iodide is less stable and decomposes easily on heating, and the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ versus $\text{I-I}$ comparison is irrelevant because those bonds are not broken during decomposition of the starting material.
options.D: The bond comparison is true, $\text{H-Cl}$ is stronger than $\text{H-I}$, but the identity is backwards. A stronger $\text{H-Cl}$ bond means hydrogen chloride is the one that is harder to decompose, not hydrogen iodide.
